subject: Linking two measures of a construct via external common items longitudinally

messages.author: 04ca78ac4f1cb8b3
messages.subject: Linking two measures of a construct via external common items longitudinally
parts:
Dear Phil,

Currently I'm working on a project where we attempt to link two measures of a construct with the hopes that we can describe the longitudinal trajectory of the construct over a relatively long timespan. Unfortunately, the measures never overlapped, but at the waves before and after the switch, a couple of items that are conceptually close to the construct and external to the measures were administered.

What I have done so far is first, estimated a GRM to the two waves of data where the switch happens, including the two external common items that occur at both waves, and saved the parameter estimates.

Then, I've fed in all the data from the two measures of interest at all time points, and then estimated another GRM using my saved parameter estimates. The external items were not included in this GRM. I then saved the factor scores for further analysis.

My questions to you are as follows:

1) Is omitting the estimation of the external items in the scoring stage correct? I reasoned that because I am trying to get an estimate of theta, I only want to include the items that are directly relevant to the construct during this stage.

2) Is it reasonable to use the factor scores I saved in a latent growth model context? I have been reading the archives of this group (and they are very helpful), and I think that I read that this is ill-advised due to shrinkage. Do you have any suggestions? Although the first goal of the project is to describe the trajectory of the construct, we would also like to predict individual differences in it with covariates.

Thank you in advance for any advice,

Joanne

parts:
On Sun, Mar 13, 2016 at 6:37 PM, Joanne Chung <chung....@gmail.com> wrote:
Dear Phil,

Currently I'm working on a project where we attempt to link two measures of a construct with the hopes that we can describe the longitudinal trajectory of the construct over a relatively long timespan. Unfortunately, the measures never overlapped, but at the waves before and after the switch, a couple of items that are conceptually close to the construct and external to the measures were administered.

That's an interesting problem. Though if the items are conceptually close, is it reasonable to constrain their parameters to be equal then? That might help to scale the parameters a bit easier if that can be justified.

What I have done so far is first, estimated a GRM to the two waves of data where the switch happens, including the two external common items that occur at both waves, and saved the parameter estimates.

Then, I've fed in all the data from the two measures of interest at all time points, and then estimated another GRM using my saved parameter estimates. The external items were not included in this GRM. I then saved the factor scores for further analysis.

My questions to you are as follows:

1) Is omitting the estimation of the external items in the scoring stage correct? I reasoned that because I am trying to get an estimate of theta, I only want to include the items that are directly relevant to the construct during this stage.
Yes this is fine.

2) Is it reasonable to use the factor scores I saved in a latent growth model context? I have been reading the archives of this group (and they are very helpful), and I think that I read that this is ill-advised due to shrinkage. Do you have any suggestions? Although the first goal of the project is to describe the trajectory of the construct, we would also like to predict individual differences in it with covariates.

It's okay to use factor scores for exploratory/suggestive reasons like this, so I wouldn't worry much. They just tend to break down when one is interested in unbiased inferences about parameters. That being said, you could always resort to plausible-value imputations to get around the problem for the most part (or at least lesson the shrinking effect), but I would do that at a later stage. Also, be sure to use MAP estimation if you have a number of latent traits (I couldn't quite tell from context). Cheers.

Phil

Thank you in advance for any advice,

Joanne
